title: The Cricket Captain: Road to the World Cup
description: Lead your team from a dusty local ground in Nagpur all the way to the ICC World Cup final. Every decision you make as captain will test your leadership — can you inspire, unite, and guide your team to glory?
cover_image_prompt: A 13-year-old Indian boy in cricket whites standing on a dusty cricket ground in Nagpur, holding a bat, looking determined at a cricket stadium in the background, vibrant watercolor illustration, warm golden light, inspiring sports story aesthetic, age 10-15 friendly
learning_objectives: Understand that leadership is about serving the team, not commanding it
Practice making decisions with incomplete or conflicting information
Develop empathy by noticing what teammates feel and need
Build resilience — learning from failures and bouncing back
Understand the difference between short-term and long-term thinking in a team
learning_concept: Great leaders are not the loudest or strongest — they are the ones who understand people, make hard calls with honesty, and lift others up even when they themselves feel uncertain.
psychological_framework: Servant Leadership (Greenleaf) — the leader's primary role is to serve the team; combined with Emotional Intelligence (Goleman) — self-awareness, empathy, and social skills

ai_image_config.style: vibrant watercolor illustration, cricket ground, Indian school and stadium settings, warm sunlight, age 10-15 friendly, inspiring sports story aesthetic

scenes.title: Surprise Captain
scenes.narrative:
Rohan had been playing cricket on this dusty ground in Nagpur since he was seven years old. The net was torn, the pitch had a crack running down the middle, and the boundary rope was really just an old garden hose. He loved every inch of it.

Today, Coach Srinivas gathered all twelve players in a circle under the big neem tree. He looked at each of them slowly, the way he always did before saying something important. Then he said, 'Rohan. You are the new captain.'

The silence was heavier than Rohan expected. He looked around. Vikram, the team's star batsman, was looking at the ground. Two other boys exchanged glances. Only his best friend Ankit was smiling. Rohan had never wanted to be captain. He just wanted to play good cricket. But now the whole team was watching him — waiting to see what he would do first.
scenes.image_prompt: A 13-year-old Indian boy named Rohan in white cricket clothes receiving a cricket captain's armband from a middle-aged coach under a large neem tree on a dusty cricket ground in Nagpur, other boys watching with mixed expressions, watercolor style, warm afternoon light, age 10-15 friendly
scenes.coaching_moment: Being chosen to lead can feel scary — just like starting anything new. The first step is usually the hardest.

choices.label: Say a few words to the team right now
choices.description: Rohan speaks up immediately, telling the team he is glad to serve them — not lead over them.

choices.label: Stay quiet and let actions speak louder
choices.description: Rohan nods quietly and picks up a bat, heading to the crease to show the team through practice.

choices.label: Ask Coach Srinivas why he chose you
choices.description: Rohan quietly asks the coach for a private word — he wants to understand what is expected of him.

scenes.title: The Team Splits
scenes.narrative:
Practice begins. Rohan watches as the team naturally breaks into two groups — those who seem okay with him as captain, and those who don't. Vikram, who has scored the most runs for the school in two years, is practising alone at the far end of the ground, hitting the ball hard against the wall.

Ankit pulls Rohan aside. 'He thinks he should have been captain,' Ankit whispers. 'His dad is on the school sports committee too.'

Rohan watches Vikram's technique. He really is good — his bat swing is beautiful. But Rohan also remembers last season, when Vikram refused to run a risky second run that could have won them a match. He was protecting his own average, Rohan had thought at the time.

Coach Srinivas is watching Rohan from the sidelines, not saying a word. Rohan knows this is a test of its own kind.
scenes.image_prompt: A split cricket practice scene — one group of boys practicing together on one side of a dusty ground, and a talented Indian boy practising alone hitting a ball against a wall on the other side, watercolor style, the new young captain watching thoughtfully, warm afternoon light, Nagpur cricket ground setting
scenes.coaching_moment: Good leaders notice when people feel left out — and they do something about it.

choices.label: Walk over to Vikram and ask him to help lead warm-ups
choices.description: Rohan gives Vikram a real responsibility — making him feel valued while bringing the team together.

choices.label: Ignore it for now and run a full team drill
choices.description: Rohan calls everyone to the middle for a fielding drill, hoping team activity dissolves the tension.

scenes.title: After Practice
scenes.narrative:
Practice is winding down. Most boys are packing their bags. Rohan notices Priya, the team manager's daughter, sitting on the boundary wall, watching with sharp eyes. She is twelve — the same age as him — and always seems to notice things adults miss.

She walks over. 'You know what the difference is between a boss and a captain?' she says. Rohan shakes his head. 'A boss says go. A captain says let's go.' She shrugs and walks away before he can respond.

Rohan stands there for a moment, watching the team trickle off the ground. Today went okay. But the District Trials are in ten days. He needs to decide how to use that time — whether to focus on individual skills, team strategy, or building trust between players. He cannot do everything.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian girl sitting on a boundary wall of a cricket ground talking to the young captain after practice, late afternoon golden light, other boys packing bags in the background, vibrant watercolor illustration, Nagpur dusty cricket ground, age 10-15 friendly
scenes.coaching_moment: Being a leader means thinking ahead — what does the team need most right now?

choices.label: Focus the next ten days on team bonding activities
choices.description: Rohan organises evening sessions — sharing snacks, telling cricket stories, building friendships first.

choices.label: Run hard tactical training sessions every day
choices.description: Rohan pushes the team through drills, fielding positions, and batting scenarios to sharpen skills.

choices.label: Mix both — bonding in the mornings, tactics in the evenings
choices.description: Rohan creates a balanced schedule, trusting that both connection and skill matter equally.

scenes.title: District Trial Morning
scenes.narrative:
The District Trials ground is nothing like Rohan's dusty patch in Nagpur. It has a proper scoreboard, a pavilion, and boys from eight different schools watching from the stands. Rohan's palms are sweating as he looks at the opposition — tall, confident players from St. Xavier's School, known for winning three consecutive district titles.

Coach Srinivas has left the batting order decision entirely to Rohan. 'You're the captain,' he said simply. Rohan has studied last month's match data. It clearly shows that Vikram scores very slowly in the first five overs — his average is 12 runs in the opening. But Vikram has stormed up to Rohan and said directly: 'I open. That's always been the deal.'

The other players are watching. This is Rohan's first real decision as captain in a match situation.
scenes.image_prompt: A proper cricket ground with a scoreboard and pavilion, a young Indian captain holding a batting order clipboard facing a confident star player who is gesturing firmly, teammates watching from the side, watercolor illustration, morning light, tense atmosphere, age 10-15 cricket setting
scenes.coaching_moment: Real decisions are rarely comfortable — but good leaders look at facts, not just feelings.

choices.label: Put Vikram at number 3 — explain it's about the team
choices.description: Rohan shows Vikram the data calmly and gives him the important anchor position instead of the opener.

choices.label: Let Vikram open — keep the peace before a big game
choices.description: Rohan decides this is not the right moment for a confrontation — the trial match is too important.

scenes.title: Runs on the Board
scenes.narrative:
The match is underway. Whatever Rohan decided, the team is now batting. By the midway point, they have a decent but not dominant score. Rohan is next to bat and he is feeling a mix of nervousness and excitement.

In the dressing room, Ankit whispers to him: 'The St. Xavier's leg spinner is getting everyone out with the same delivery — a quicker one that drifts in. I watched three of their matches. Every batsman is scared of the short ball too. If you can get Vikram to play the spinner aggressively, it might change the whole match.'

Rohan thinks. The plan makes sense. But asking Vikram to change his natural game mid-match is risky — if it fails, Vikram will blame Rohan. Rohan could also trust the team to play their natural game. Or he could try to go speak to Vikram himself at the break.
scenes.image_prompt: Inside a cricket dressing room with young Indian players, a boy whispering a tactical plan to the young captain who is padded up to bat, chalkboard with fielding positions on the wall, watercolor illustration, dressing room atmosphere, age 10-15 cricket story
scenes.coaching_moment: Good strategies only work if you can get people to believe in them — communication is part of leadership.

choices.label: Speak to Vikram directly with Ankit's analysis
choices.description: Rohan pulls Vikram aside and shares the observations — giving him the information and letting him decide.

choices.label: Trust the team to play naturally — no mid-match changes
choices.description: Rohan decides that changing tactics under pressure creates more panic than it solves.

choices.label: Ask Coach Srinivas for his opinion first
choices.description: Rohan knows he doesn't have all the answers — and a good leader knows when to seek advice.

scenes.title: Last Over
scenes.narrative:
The final over arrives. Rohan's team needs 14 runs to win. It is very tight. Rohan is not batting — he is watching from the boundary, hands clasped, stomach in a knot.

The batsman at the crease hits a four, then a single. Another four. Then a wicket falls. Now it is 5 runs needed off the last 3 balls, and the new batsman is nervous Arjun, who has barely played in the school team before. The crowd has gone quiet.

Whatever happens in the next three balls, the match is nearly over. Rohan watches Arjun look back at him from the crease, seeking some signal, some reassurance. What does the captain do in this moment?
scenes.image_prompt: A tense cricket match final over — a nervous young batsman at the crease looking back at the boundary for guidance, the young captain at the boundary edge making a gesture, spectators watching anxiously, watercolor illustration, stadium atmosphere, late afternoon light, age 10-15 cricket story
scenes.coaching_moment: A captain's job doesn't stop when they are not batting — the team is always watching for reassurance.

choices.label: Give Arjun a big thumbs up and point forward — trust him
choices.description: Rohan shows Arjun he believes in him completely, giving him the confidence to back himself.

choices.label: Signal a specific shot — hit it over mid-on
choices.description: Rohan gives a tactical instruction, trusting that a clear plan will calm Arjun's nerves.

scenes.title: The Abandoned Match
scenes.narrative:
Three days after the district trials, the weather turns. Dark clouds roll in from the west, and the afternoon match against Vidyanagar School is abandoned after just fifteen overs. The boys are frustrated — they were winning — but there is nothing to do about the rain.

As the team shelters under the pavilion roof, Rohan notices something. Dev, one of their best all-rounders, is sitting alone at the far end of the bench. Dev has been quiet all week. Not just today. He has been getting out to easy balls, missing catches he would normally take in his sleep, and arriving late to practice twice.

Rohan thinks back. Dev's mother had been ill — he had mentioned it briefly three weeks ago and then never brought it up again. Everyone had moved on. But Rohan wonders now if Dev had moved on at all.
scenes.image_prompt: A cricket pavilion during rain, young Indian players sheltering under the roof, one boy sitting alone at the far end of a bench looking sad and withdrawn while others talk loudly, young captain noticing him, watercolor illustration, rainy day mood, warm indoor light contrasting with dark skies outside
scenes.coaching_moment: Being a good leader means noticing what people are NOT saying — sometimes that is the loudest message of all.

choices.label: Go sit next to Dev — just be there, say nothing yet
choices.description: Rohan walks over and sits beside Dev without saying anything — just being present is sometimes enough.

choices.label: Ask Dev directly if everything is okay at home
choices.description: Rohan decides honesty is kinder than pretending not to notice — he asks Dev quietly and directly.

choices.label: Tell Coach Srinivas — a captain can ask for help too
choices.description: Rohan recognises this is beyond cricket — he loops in the coach who knows the team better.

scenes.title: Dev Opens Up
scenes.narrative:
Whatever Rohan chose, it works. Dev begins to talk. His mother has been in hospital in Amravati. His father is working extra shifts. Dev has been taking a bus home alone every evening, cooking for his younger sister, and then trying to do homework.

'I didn't want to make it anyone's problem,' Dev says quietly. 'You all have enough to worry about with the trials.'

Rohan feels something shift inside him. He had been thinking about Dev as a 'problem player' this past week — someone who needed to play better. But that was completely wrong. Dev wasn't struggling at cricket. He was struggling with life.

The rain hammers down on the pavilion roof. The other players are talking and laughing at the other end — none of them know what is happening here. Rohan has to decide what to do with what he now knows.
scenes.image_prompt: Two young Indian boys having a quiet conversation at the far end of a pavilion bench during heavy rain, one boy looking down and talking, the other listening carefully with concern, other teammates laughing in the background unaware, watercolor illustration, warm and empathetic mood, age 10-15 friendly
scenes.coaching_moment: When someone shares something hard with you, the most powerful thing you can do is truly listen — not rush to fix it.

choices.label: Promise Dev the team will have his back — then tell the team
choices.description: Rohan asks Dev's permission and then shares with the team, rallying them to support Dev quietly.

choices.label: Keep it between Rohan and Dev — respect his privacy
choices.description: Rohan promises Dev it stays between them, and finds small ways to quietly ease the load without a big announcement.

scenes.title: What the Coach Said
scenes.narrative:
The rain stops. The ground is waterlogged and unplayable, so practice is cancelled. As the team prepares to leave, Coach Srinivas pulls Rohan aside.

'I saw what you did with Dev,' the coach says. He doesn't say how — the coach always seems to see everything. 'That was good captaincy. Better than any bowling change you could have made today.'

Rohan isn't sure what to say. He hadn't done it to be a good captain. He had done it because Dev was his teammate and something was wrong.

'That is exactly why it was good captaincy,' Coach Srinivas says, as if reading his mind. 'When you lead because you care, not because you want the credit — that is when people really follow you.'

Rohan walks home in the drizzle, thinking about something Priya said last week: a captain says 'let's go.' Not just on the field. In life too.
scenes.image_prompt: A wise middle-aged Indian cricket coach having a quiet, meaningful conversation with a young captain on a rain-wet cricket ground, puddles reflecting late afternoon light, the boy listening thoughtfully, other players walking away in the distance, watercolor illustration, inspiring mood
scenes.coaching_moment: Leadership that comes from caring about people is more powerful than leadership that comes from wanting to be in charge.

choices.label: Ask Coach Srinivas how he knows when to trust his instincts
choices.description: Rohan takes the moment to learn from his coach — asking the deeper question behind the compliment.

choices.label: Thank Coach quietly and head home to think
choices.description: Rohan absorbs the lesson in silence, reflecting on what leadership really means as he walks.

scenes.title: The State Team Announcement
scenes.narrative:
The State Under-15 Selection Committee has announced that one player from Rohan's school will be given a trial spot for the Maharashtra state team. Coach Srinivas has told Rohan that he gets to recommend the name — a huge responsibility.

The two obvious candidates are Ankit, Rohan's loyal best friend who has worked harder than anyone all season, and Sanjay, a talented new student from Pune who joined the school three months ago. Sanjay is technically better — his bowling average is 14 compared to Ankit's 22. But Sanjay is arrogant, clashes with teammates, and once refused to bowl in a match because he disagreed with Rohan's field placement.

Ankit knows he is being considered. He has not asked Rohan directly, but Rohan can see the hope in his eyes every time the topic comes up. The recommendation is due tomorrow morning.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian captain sitting alone at a desk looking at two sets of cricket statistics on paper — one marked with a loyal friend's name and one with a skilled but difficult player — a difficult decision moment, watercolor illustration, evening light, thoughtful and serious mood, age 10-15
scenes.coaching_moment: Some of the hardest decisions in leadership are the ones between what is fair and what is comfortable.

choices.label: Recommend Sanjay — skill should come first in trials
choices.description: Rohan chooses merit, knowing it will hurt Ankit but believing the team's future matters most.

choices.label: Recommend Ankit — loyalty and effort deserve reward
choices.description: Rohan chooses his friend, believing that trust and consistency are qualities that matter in a team player.

choices.label: Ask Coach Srinivas to help you think it through together
choices.description: Rohan decides not to carry this alone — he asks for a second perspective before deciding.

scenes.title: Ankit's Reaction
scenes.narrative:
Whatever Rohan decides, Ankit finds out the next morning. If Rohan chose Sanjay, Ankit is devastated but tries to hide it behind a quiet nod. If Rohan chose Ankit, Sanjay storms off without a word. Either way, Rohan must now deal with the consequence in the dressing room before the next practice.

The team can feel the tension. Two or three players are looking at Rohan differently — some with respect, some with doubt. Priya, who has been helping with scorecards, catches Rohan's eye as he walks in. She gives him a small nod that seems to say: whatever you decided, you have to own it now.

Rohan stands at the front of the dressing room. He can either explain his thinking to the team, or get straight into the warm-up and hope the tension dissolves through activity.
scenes.image_prompt: Inside a school cricket dressing room, young Indian players looking at their captain with mixed expressions — some supportive, some uncertain, one boy looking away hurt — the captain standing at the front about to speak, watercolor illustration, tense but hopeful atmosphere
scenes.coaching_moment: After making a hard decision, a leader needs the courage to stand by it — and explain the thinking honestly.

choices.label: Explain your reasoning to the whole team honestly
choices.description: Rohan tells the team how he made the decision and what criteria he used — complete transparency.

choices.label: Speak to Ankit or Sanjay privately first, then address the team
choices.description: Rohan handles the personal impact before the group one — fixing the root before the branch.

scenes.title: After the Storm
scenes.narrative:
The team practice that afternoon is quieter than usual, but something feels more settled. When a hard decision is made and owned, people tend to adjust faster than you expect.

Late in the practice, Coach Srinivas sits next to Rohan on the boundary. 'Meritocracy,' the coach says quietly. 'It is a good word. But do you know what it means to make a meritocracy work? You have to make the criteria clear BEFORE the decision — not after. Otherwise people think you chose the criteria to match who you already wanted to pick.'

Rohan stares at the ground. He hadn't thought of it that way. The coach continues: 'Next time — before a selection is announced — write down what the criteria are. Post it on the wall. Then people trust the process, not just the person.'

Rohan pulls out his notebook and writes: Make the rules before the game, not after.
scenes.image_prompt: A wise coach and a young captain sitting side by side on a cricket ground boundary in late afternoon light, the boy writing in a small notebook, thoughtful and reflective moment, watercolor illustration, Nagpur setting, warm golden light, age 10-15 friendly
scenes.coaching_moment: Fairness is not just about the decision you make — it is about making the rules clear before the game begins.

choices.label: Write down your selection criteria and share it with the team
choices.description: Rohan decides to act on the coach's lesson immediately — pinning criteria on the dressing room wall.

choices.label: Keep the lesson in your notebook — act on it next time
choices.description: Rohan absorbs the advice but feels the moment has passed for this particular group.

scenes.title: Half-Time in the Semi-Final
scenes.narrative:
The zonal semi-final. 200 runs needed off the last 20 overs. The team is batting but has lost three wickets cheaply. The dressing room at the break is thick with silence. Some players are staring at the floor. Dev is tying and untying his shoelaces. Vikram looks rigid with anger.

Coach Srinivas steps back deliberately — he is giving Rohan the floor. This is Rohan's team talk to give. All eleven players are looking at him.

Rohan's heart is hammering. He wants to say the right thing. He remembers reading once about how great half-time speeches work: not by listing what went wrong, but by reminding people of who they are and what they are capable of. But he also knows he only has five minutes.
scenes.image_prompt: Inside a cricket dressing room during half-time, young Indian players sitting on benches looking dejected or tense, the young captain standing and about to speak, some teammates looking at him with hope, watercolor illustration, tense but charged atmosphere, indoor light, age 10-15 cricket story
scenes.coaching_moment: When people are scared or down, they don't need a list of what went wrong — they need to be reminded of what they are capable of.

choices.label: Focus on what went well first — then what to change
choices.description: Rohan starts with two things the team did right, then calmly addresses the adjustments needed.

choices.label: Be brutally honest — tell them exactly what went wrong
choices.description: Rohan lays it out clearly — no sugar-coating, just the facts and what needs to change.

choices.label: Tell a story — remind them why they love this game
choices.description: Rohan shares a memory from early in the season — reconnecting the team to their passion, not the scoreboard.

scenes.title: The Batting Plan
scenes.narrative:
The team talk has helped — the energy in the dressing room has shifted. Players are sitting straighter. Vikram has uncrossed his arms. Dev even cracked a small smile.

Now Rohan needs to make one more decision before they head back out. Looking at the required run rate, there are two possible approaches. The first is conservative: rotate the strike, keep wickets in hand, and build pressure late. The second is aggressive: send the best strikers up the order and try to take the game on from ball one.

Ankit pulls Rohan aside: 'The opposition's best bowler is only allowed four overs. He has two left. If we attack in his last two overs, he might get expensive. After that, their bowling is much weaker.'

Rohan has two minutes to decide the batting plan and communicate it to the team.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian cricket players gathered around their captain in a dressing room doorway, the captain drawing a quick plan on a small whiteboard, some players nodding, others looking tense, watercolor illustration, about-to-step-out-on-field energy, age 10-15 cricket setting
scenes.coaching_moment: The best plans are simple enough to remember under pressure — and brave enough to actually try.

choices.label: Use Ankit's insight — target the star bowler's last two overs
choices.description: Rohan builds the plan around the data Ankit gathered — attacking the weakest point strategically.

choices.label: Play conservative — build to a strong final five overs
choices.description: Rohan trusts the slower, safer approach — keeping wickets in hand for a late assault.

scenes.title: Winning the Semi-Final
scenes.narrative:
The second innings unfolds. There are moments of brilliance, one wobble in the middle where two wickets fall in three balls, and then a magnificent last-over partnership between Vikram and Dev that nobody expected.

When the winning run is scored, the team erupts. Dev punches the air. Vikram — even Vikram — is grinning. Rohan stands at the boundary edge, feeling something he cannot quite name. It is not just happiness. It is something bigger.

Priya runs across the ground towards the celebrating players, scorebook in hand. She stops next to Rohan for a moment. 'You know what you did in that dressing room?' she says. 'You made them believe the story wasn't over yet. That is what a captain does.'

Rohan watches his team celebrate. For the first time since being handed the armband, he feels — not just responsible — but proud.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian cricket players celebrating a semi-final win on a proper cricket ground, jumping and hugging each other, the young captain watching his team celebrate with a big smile, watercolor illustration, sunset colors, joyful and triumphant mood, age 10-15 cricket story
scenes.coaching_moment: The best reward of leadership is not winning — it is watching people you believed in become more than they thought they could be.

choices.label: Rush into the celebrations and celebrate with the team
choices.description: Rohan lets himself be part of the joy — a captain who celebrates with the team, not above them.

choices.label: Make sure you acknowledge every single player — even the ones who didn't bat
choices.description: Rohan goes around the whole team, making sure every player feels part of the win.

scenes.title: The Strategy Document
scenes.narrative:
Two days before the state finals, Rohan arrives at the opposition dressing room by mistake — a mix-up with the ground allocation. Nobody is there. On the bench, a folder has been left open. Rohan glances at it and realises immediately what it is: the opposing team's full tactical plan. Their set plays, their weaknesses, their field placements.

His first instinct is to look away and leave. His second instinct is less clear. This information could be the difference between winning and losing. He knows where Ankit and Vikram are — he could tell them. Nobody would know. The folder was left open; he didn't break into anything.

He stares at the folder for several seconds. His hands are very still.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian cricket captain alone in a dressing room, looking at an open folder with tactics written inside that was clearly left by mistake, looking conflicted and serious, watercolor illustration, indoor light, moral dilemma moment, age 10-15 cricket story, no villains — just a hard choice
scenes.coaching_moment: Integrity means doing the right thing even when nobody is watching — and even when it costs you something.

choices.label: Close the folder and leave immediately — don't even read it
choices.description: Rohan turns and walks away without looking at a single word. Clean conscience, clean hands.

choices.label: Read it quickly, then leave — just information
choices.description: Rohan glances at the key points before leaving. The information is already in his head now.

choices.label: Take it to the match official and report it was left behind
choices.description: Rohan picks it up carefully and takes it to the match officials, reporting the situation honestly.

scenes.title: Vikram Asks
scenes.narrative:
Later that afternoon, Vikram comes to Rohan with a smirk. 'Someone told me you were in their dressing room. Did you see anything useful?'

Rohan understands immediately what Vikram wants. Vikram is not asking out of curiosity — he is asking because he would have looked if it were him, and he is testing whether Rohan did too.

The way Rohan answers this question will ripple through the team. If he lies, the team will never know. If he tells the truth, either they will respect him or question whether he made the right call. Priya is nearby, pretending to read a scorebook but definitely listening.
scenes.image_prompt: Two young Indian cricket players in a half-lit dressing room corridor, the star batsman asking the captain a loaded question with a sly expression, the captain looking directly back at him with calm eyes, Priya visible in the background pretending to read, watercolor illustration, charged moment
scenes.coaching_moment: How you respond when tested by someone who expects you to do the wrong thing says everything about your character.

choices.label: Tell Vikram exactly what happened — and what you decided
choices.description: Rohan is completely honest with Vikram, explaining what he found and what he did about it.

choices.label: Say simply: I didn't use anything I shouldn't have
choices.description: Rohan gives a clear, short answer — honest but not inviting a longer debate.

scenes.title: What the Team Learns
scenes.narrative:
Word spreads through the team — as it always does. Whether Rohan read the folder or didn't, what he did or said afterward becomes the team's story about who their captain is.

Coach Srinivas finds out too. He says nothing about the folder directly. Instead, at the end of practice, he gathers the team and says: 'There is a concept in sport called the spirit of the game. It is different from the rules of the game. Rules tell you what you cannot do. Spirit tells you what you should do even when the rules don't require it. The best teams play by the spirit, not just the rules.'

He looks at Rohan briefly. Not with praise or criticism. Just with a look that says: the score will be settled in the long run, not today.
scenes.image_prompt: A cricket coach giving a quiet talk to a team of young players sitting in a circle on the grass near the boundary, the sun setting behind the cricket ground, each player listening carefully, watercolor illustration, thoughtful and reflective mood, Nagpur cricket ground setting
scenes.coaching_moment: The rules tell you what you must do. Your values tell you what you choose to do.

choices.label: Speak to the team about what the spirit of the game means to you
choices.description: Rohan takes the coach's cue and adds his own voice — being vulnerable and honest with his team.

choices.label: Let Coach's words stand — add action, not speeches
choices.description: Rohan decides to show the team through how he plays rather than another speech.

scenes.title: Coach's Story
scenes.narrative:
The night before the state finals, Coach Srinivas gathers the team not on the cricket ground, but at a nearby community hall. There are no bats or balls. He sits them down and says: 'I want to tell you a story.'

He describes his younger days, when he was a trekker. He had once been part of a team attempting to reach a base camp on a Himalayan peak. They had sixty days and very limited supplies. The goal seemed impossibly far.

'The worst thing you can do on a long climb,' Coach Srinivas says, 'is look at the peak. It is too far away. It paralyses you. So what do we do instead?' He pauses. 'We look at the next two hours. Just the next two hours. What do we need to do in the next two hours to make tomorrow possible?'

Rohan writes in his notebook: Break the impossible into the next two hours.
scenes.image_prompt: A wise Indian cricket coach telling a mountain climbing story to a group of attentive young players sitting cross-legged in a community hall at night, a hand-drawn mountain diagram on a chalkboard behind him, lantern light, watercolor illustration, warm and wise storytelling atmosphere, age 10-15
scenes.coaching_moment: Big goals are not reached in one leap — they are reached two hours at a time.

choices.label: Ask: What are our 'next two hours' before tomorrow's final?
choices.description: Rohan applies the idea immediately — he steers the team to think in small steps for match day.

choices.label: Ask Coach what happened on his climb — did he make it?
choices.description: Rohan wants the whole story — he knows the team does too, and connection matters tonight.

scenes.title: The Mountain That Never Ends
scenes.narrative:
Coach Srinivas continues his story. He reaches the part where, after forty days of climbing, a storm hit. Three team members had to turn back. The base camp they were aiming for was now out of reach. The team had a choice: declare failure or redefine success.

'We redefined success,' he says quietly. 'We set a new target — a ridge camp, three days below the original base camp. We got there. It wasn't what we planned. But we all came home. And the next season, we tried again and we got further.'

Rohan looks at his teammates. The finals are tomorrow. What if they don't win? What is the new definition of success? He starts to think about this differently — not as failure risk, but as learning opportunity.

Dev raises his hand: 'Coach — is the World Cup our Everest base camp, or is it just one more ridge camp along the way?'

Everyone is quiet. It is a beautiful question.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian cricket players sitting in a community hall listening intently to a coach's story about mountain climbing, one boy raising his hand to ask a thoughtful question, the group looking contemplative and inspired, watercolor illustration, warm lamplight, meaningful evening before a big day
scenes.coaching_moment: Success is not always reaching the peak — sometimes it is reaching as far as you honestly can and learning for next time.

choices.label: Answer Dev: 'It's both — and either way, we keep climbing'
choices.description: Rohan gives the team a frame for tomorrow: win or lose, this is one step on a longer journey.

choices.label: Let Coach answer — he told the story for a reason
choices.description: Rohan reads the room and lets the wiser voice speak — another way of leading.

scenes.title: The Team Pact
scenes.narrative:
The session ends with something Rohan had not planned. Ankit suggests each player write one thing on a piece of paper — the single thing they will focus on tomorrow, not for themselves but for the team. They fold the papers and Rohan collects them.

When he reads them later that night, alone in his room, he finds things like: 'I'll back up every run.' 'I won't drop my head if I get out.' 'I'll cheer louder than anyone.' Even Vikram has written something: 'I'll trust the plan.'

Rohan sits for a long time with these small pieces of paper in his hand. Tomorrow they play the state final. He doesn't know if they will win. But for the first time since being made captain, he is completely sure of one thing: this team is ready.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian captain sitting alone in his room at night, reading small pieces of folded paper from his teammates, a lamp on the desk, a cricket bat propped in the corner, warm watercolor illustration, quiet and meaningful mood, age 10-15 leadership story
scenes.coaching_moment: When a team shows up for each other, not just for the scoreboard — that is when real strength appears.

choices.label: Write your own paper and add it to the stack — you're part of the team too
choices.description: Rohan writes his own commitment and adds it to the pile — the captain is not above the team.

choices.label: Read them all again and think about what each player needs tomorrow
choices.description: Rohan uses the papers as preparation — understanding each player so he can captain well tomorrow.

scenes.title: India U-15 Trials
scenes.narrative:
Rohan's performance in the state finals has caught the attention of selectors. He has been invited to the India Under-15 national trials in Mumbai — along with twenty-three other players from across the country. It is the biggest moment of his cricket life.

The trials ground is in Bandra. Players have arrived from Kerala, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, and Rajasthan. They play differently. The Kerala boys have technically perfect defensive strokes. The Punjab batsmen are aggressive from ball one. The Assam player in the nets does something Rohan has never seen — he sweeps the ball even on a full length. Every team has a different style.

Rohan watches all of this before the first day's practice even begins. He is used to one way of playing. His whole cricket education has been built on the Nagpur way. Now he needs to think: how do you adapt without losing who you are?
scenes.image_prompt: A cricket net session at a large Mumbai training ground, young players from different Indian states with different styles all practising together, the young captain from Nagpur watching with curiosity and adjustment, coaches with clipboards, vibrant watercolor illustration, Mumbai cricket grounds, diverse group of players
scenes.coaching_moment: Meeting people who do things differently is not a threat — it is the fastest way to grow.

choices.label: Watch carefully and try to pick up one new technique from each state
choices.description: Rohan decides to actively learn — treating every different player as a teacher.

choices.label: Focus on your own game — play your strengths under pressure
choices.description: Rohan decides that consistency in his own style is more important than trying to be everything.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to players from two other states — build connections first
choices.description: Rohan knows that cricket is partly about reading people — he invests in relationships early.

scenes.title: The National Captain's Call
scenes.narrative:
On the second day of trials, the coaches pull Rohan aside. They are not discussing his individual performance. They are asking him a question: 'If you were made captain of this combined India U-15 trial team for a practice match tomorrow, what would you do differently here than with your school team?'

Rohan thinks hard. This team has players who barely know each other. They have completely different styles. They may speak different languages. The things that worked with his Nagpur school team — the inside jokes, the shared history, Dev's loyalty, Ankit's quiet support — none of that exists here yet.

He has one evening to prepare a leadership approach for a team of strangers.
scenes.image_prompt: A young cricket captain sitting across from two national team coaches with clipboards in a small meeting room at a Mumbai cricket academy, a diverse group of young players visible through the window practicing in the nets, thoughtful expression on the boy's face, watercolor illustration, serious but exciting atmosphere
scenes.coaching_moment: Leadership that works in one context must be adapted — not abandoned — when the context changes.

choices.label: Create a quick shared ritual — a team handshake or word before taking the field
choices.description: Rohan knows that small shared moments build fast bonds — he designs one for the morning.

choices.label: Let everyone play their natural game — no forced team style
choices.description: Rohan respects that each player has a different background and should not be squeezed into one mould.

scenes.title: One Team, Many Voices
scenes.narrative:
The practice match is played. Rohan captains this unfamiliar, diverse group for a full thirty-over game. There are moments of confusion — a miscommunication between a player from Assam and one from Punjab leads to a dropped catch — and moments of brilliance that Rohan could never have anticipated.

Afterward, one of the coaches tells the group something that Rohan writes down in his notebook: 'The India team is only as strong as its diversity. If every player thinks the same way, a good opposition will predict you every time. But if your team has ten different ways of seeing the game, you are unpredictable.'

On the train back to Nagpur, Rohan stares out the window at the Western Ghats rolling past. He is thinking about his school team differently now — not as players who should do things his way, but as players whose different ways make the team harder to beat.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian cricket captain looking thoughtfully out of a train window at the passing landscape of the Western Ghats, his reflection visible in the glass, a small notebook in his hand, watercolor illustration, late afternoon light, contemplative mood, growth and reflection moment, age 10-15
scenes.coaching_moment: A team's strength does not come from everyone being the same — it comes from different people knowing how to work together.

choices.label: Write a note to each team member about what makes them special
choices.description: Rohan spends the train ride writing short personal notes — celebrating each player's unique quality.

choices.label: Plan the World Cup squad selection using everything learned at the trials
choices.description: Rohan uses his new perspective to think about which combinations make the team hardest to predict.

scenes.title: The Night Before
scenes.narrative:
It is the night before the ICC Under-15 World Cup Final. India vs. Australia. The tournament has been in Sri Lanka. Rohan is lying awake in the team hotel at 1am, staring at the ceiling.

He has been replaying every decision he has made this year. The batting order fight with Vikram. The selection between Ankit and Sanjay. Dev and the rainy pavilion. The folder left open in the dressing room. The papers the team wrote the night before the state final.

All of it has led to here. But there is one more decision waiting for him in the morning, and it is the hardest one: Dev has a partial muscle strain. The physio says he can play, but there is a real risk of serious injury if he pushes too hard. Dev desperately wants to play. It is the World Cup Final. But Rohan could protect him — bench him, keep him safe, let another player take his place.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian cricket captain lying awake in a hotel room at night, the ceiling above him, his cricket kit visible in the corner, a soft lamp on, thinking deeply, watercolor illustration, quiet and reflective mood, the weight of a big decision visible in his expression, age 10-15
scenes.coaching_moment: Servant leadership means sometimes making decisions that protect people even when they don't want to be protected.

choices.label: Talk to Dev tonight — be honest about the risk and decide together
choices.description: Rohan knocks on Dev's door at 1am and has an honest conversation — sharing the decision rather than carrying it alone.

choices.label: Decide to bench Dev — the captain's job is to protect the team
choices.description: Rohan makes the hard call alone — protecting Dev even though Dev will be angry and disappointed.

choices.label: Let Dev play — respect his right to decide for himself
choices.description: Rohan trusts Dev's judgment about his own body — a different form of respect.

scenes.title: Dev's Answer
scenes.narrative:
Dev has listened to whatever Rohan said. Now it is Dev's turn to speak. He tells Rohan about his mother, who is now recovering well. He tells him about the bus rides home, the dinners he cooked for his sister, the homework done at midnight.

'I have already played the hardest match of my life,' Dev says quietly. 'This is just cricket. Let me play.'

There is something in the way Dev says it — not desperate, not dramatic, but certain. He is not asking for permission. He is telling Rohan something about himself that he has never said in words before: I am stronger than you think.

Rohan sits with this. The physio said there is a risk. But the physio also said Dev can play. Between a medical clearance and a broken spirit, which costs the team more?
scenes.image_prompt: Two young Indian cricket teammates having an honest late-night conversation in a hotel corridor, one looking determined and calm, the other listening carefully and weighing up the decision, soft corridor light, watercolor illustration, emotional and meaningful moment, team trust and friendship, age 10-15
scenes.coaching_moment: Sometimes the people we try to protect are already stronger than we realise — and seeing that is a form of respect.

choices.label: Trust Dev — let him play, but have the substitute ready just in case
choices.description: Rohan honours Dev's decision and also prepares a backup — responsible trust.

choices.label: Still bench Dev — a captain's job is to see beyond the moment
choices.description: Rohan cares too much about Dev's long-term health to let the final decide it — even at the cost of their relationship tonight.

scenes.title: Match Day Morning
scenes.narrative:
Match day morning. The hotel lobby fills with the sound of players eating breakfast, coaches murmuring to each other, the distant sound of the stadium being prepared. The sky outside is bright and clear.

Rohan eats quietly with Vikram, who has transformed over this year. The arrogance has not disappeared — it is still there in the set of his jaw and the way he sizes up opposition bowlers — but it has been tempered. He and Rohan have not become best friends. But they have become something better: people who trust each other on the field.

'Whatever happens today,' Vikram says between mouthfuls of idli, 'this was a good team.'

Rohan nods. It was. It is. Win or lose, something was built this year that will last longer than any scoreboard.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian cricket players eating breakfast together in a bright hotel dining room on the morning of a World Cup Final, a mix of nervous and excited energy, some players laughing, some quiet, the young captain eating with the star batsman in a moment of quiet mutual respect, watercolor illustration, warm morning light
scenes.coaching_moment: The work of building something real — a team, a friendship, a habit — outlasts any single result.

choices.label: Give the team a short, honest pre-match talk — no speeches, just truth
choices.description: Rohan gathers the team for five minutes and says simply: 'Play for each other today. That is enough.'

choices.label: Say nothing extra — the preparation has already been done
choices.description: Rohan trusts that everything needed has already been said and done — the team is ready.

scenes.title: The World Cup Final
scenes.narrative:
The ICC Under-15 World Cup Final. India vs. Australia. 5,000 supporters in the stands, broadcasters, cameras. Rohan wins the toss and has to decide: bat or bowl first?

The pitch looks fresh and slightly damp. The Australian fast bowling unit is their strength — they are big, quick, and accurate. Rohan knows that facing them in the first fifteen overs while the pitch is fresh is a serious risk. But batting second under pressure, chasing a target, is also hard.

Coach Srinivas has not given him a recommendation. The captain decides. Rohan looks at the sky, feels the slight moisture in the breeze, and checks the pitch one last time. The umpires are waiting. The stadium is buzzing.
scenes.image_prompt: A 13-year-old Indian cricket captain in whites at the centre of a cricket stadium at the toss, facing the Australian captain, umpires in white coats watching, a large crowd in the background, watercolor illustration, bright stadium atmosphere, the biggest moment of the young captain's life, inspiring and tense
scenes.coaching_moment: Even in the biggest moments, the best captains trust the thinking they have done — not the fear they feel.

choices.label: Bat first — build a target and let your bowlers defend it
choices.description: Rohan chooses to put runs on the board and back the bowlers to defend under pressure.

choices.label: Bowl first — use the damp pitch against the Australian batsmen
choices.description: Rohan decides to negate Australia's fast bowling strength by making them bat in the better conditions.

scenes.title: Last Over
scenes.narrative:
The match has been extraordinary. It has swung three times. India are batting, chasing 187. They need 14 runs off the last over. Vikram is at the crease, 67 not out, one of the best innings Rohan has seen from him all year. But the Australian captain has a decision to make too — and he brings on his fastest bowler for the last over.

Rohan is at the non-striker's end. He has scored 31 — enough, but not a match-winning knock. The last over begins. He watches Vikram's body language. Tight jaw, but eyes completely focused. Four off the first ball. Two off the second. A dot ball. A single — Rohan takes it, and now Rohan is facing the last three balls. 7 runs needed.

From the boundary, Coach Srinivas is still. He will not call anything. This is Rohan's game.
scenes.image_prompt: A dramatic cricket match final over — a young Indian batsman facing a fast delivery in a packed stadium, the other young Indian batsman watching from the non-striker's end, the crowd blurred but enormous in the background, watercolor illustration, high-intensity sports moment, sunset stadium light
scenes.coaching_moment: Pressure reveals character — and the character built over a whole year is what shows up in the last over.

choices.label: Go for the big shot — trust the preparation, back yourself
choices.description: Rohan decides the moment calls for courage — he goes for the boundary, all or nothing.

choices.label: Keep it smart — rotate strike, let the last ball decide
choices.description: Rohan trusts his training, picks gaps, and takes it one ball at a time.

scenes.title: Whatever the Score
scenes.narrative:
The last ball is bowled. Whether India wins or loses by the narrowest of margins, something remarkable has happened today. The team played like they wrote on those folded pieces of paper. Dev — played or benched — was part of every celebration and every low moment. Vikram played for the team, not for his average. Ankit backed up every single run.

If India wins, the ground erupts. If India loses by a thin margin, there is silence — and then, slowly, a strange kind of peace. Because Rohan knows, and the team knows, that they left everything on the ground.

Coach Srinivas finds Rohan in the crowd afterward — win or lose — and says one sentence: 'A captain is remembered not for trophies. He is remembered for how he made people feel about themselves.'

Rohan looks at his team — laughing, crying, exhausted, proud — and realises that something bigger than a trophy was won today. A group of twelve-year-olds from Nagpur became, briefly, exactly who they were always capable of being.
scenes.image_prompt: The aftermath of a cricket World Cup Final — young Indian players in a circle on the pitch, some celebrating, some with heads bowed, the young captain in the middle with both arms around two teammates, the coach watching proudly from the side, watercolor illustration, golden stadium lights, emotional and triumphant mood regardless of result
scenes.coaching_moment: Win or lose, what you built together — the trust, the honesty, the care — that is yours to keep forever.

choices.label: Gather the team in a circle right there on the pitch
choices.description: Rohan calls the whole team together on the field — win or lose, they finish as one.
choices.ending_message: Whatever the scoreboard says, Rohan and his team walked off that pitch knowing they had built something real. A captain who led by caring, who made hard calls with honesty, and who always, always put the team first. The trophy can only go to one team. But the kind of captain Rohan became — that belongs to everyone who played with him.

choices.label: Go shake hands with every Australian player first
choices.description: Rohan walks to the opposition and offers genuine handshakes — the spirit of the game, lived out loud.
choices.ending_message: Rohan shook every hand that day — opponents first, then teammates, then the people in the stands who had never met him but believed in him. Years later, the players who were on that field would remember the score less and less. But they would always remember the captain who showed them what it really meant to play with heart.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to guide and inspire a group of people towards a common goal — not by commanding, but by earning trust and showing the way.
The leader of a team — responsible not just for decisions, but for how the team feels, works together, and grows.
A plan for how to achieve a goal — thinking several steps ahead and making choices based on what you know.
Doing the right thing even when no one is watching, and even when it costs you something.
The ability to understand and share what another person is feeling — putting yourself in their shoes.
Giving part of your responsibility to someone else — trusting them to do it, and freeing you to focus on other things.
The reason or energy that drives someone to try hard and keep going — it can come from inside (wanting to achieve something) or outside (wanting a reward).
The ability to bounce back after something goes wrong — not pretending the setback didn't happen, but choosing to keep going anyway.
Believing that someone will do what they said they would do, and that they have your interests at heart.
Sharing information and ideas clearly with others — including listening as much as speaking.
A system where people are chosen or rewarded based on their skill and effort, not on who they know or how popular they are.
Information about how someone did — honest, specific, and meant to help them improve, not to make them feel bad.
A clear picture of where you are trying to go — a goal far enough in the future that it inspires people.
Working together with others towards a shared goal — combining everyone's strengths and covering each other's weaknesses.
The stress that comes when a lot is at stake — good leaders learn to perform under pressure without panicking.
The process of choosing between different options — gathering information, weighing the options, and picking the best one you can.
Taking responsibility for your own choices and actions — owning the outcome, whether it goes well or badly.
Treating others with consideration and recognising their value as people — regardless of their status or skill.
Being a leader who works FOR the team, not the other way around — like a captain who carries the kit bag so others can rest.
When everyone in a team feels safe enough to speak up, ask questions, or make mistakes without being embarrassed or punished — it makes teams braver and better.

coaching_moment: Leadership is not about being the best player — it is about bringing out the best in everyone around you.
reflection_prompt: Looking back at the choices you made, which one felt hardest and why? What would you do differently if you replayed?
